title: Openrouter will scan all traffic, adds human review
content:
CSAM Screening Across OpenRouter
OpenRouter ·
OpenRouter will screen all inference requests for child sexual abuse material (CSAM) as they pass through our service. Screening happens in flight, during request processing. Content flagged as potential CSAM may be retained for human review, with reporting and preservation where required by law.
How CSAM screening will work
- Known CSAM detection. In-flight screening will include comparing applicable content against hashes (digital fingerprints) of previously identified CSAM.
- Review of suspected new CSAM. We may begin retaining content flagged as potential CSAM for human review, including content that does not match a known hash. A flag indicates suspected material; it is not itself a determination that the content is CSAM.
Hash matching detects known material, while classifiers can identify suspected material that has not yet been added to a hash database. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) recommends hashing and image classifiers as basic child-safety measures for services handling images and video, including generative AI services (NCMEC’s guidance).
Screening also applies to ZDR traffic
CSAM screening will also apply to requests covered by OpenRouter’s Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policy.
We’re updating our documentation and related terms to make OpenRouter’s own retention commitment explicit:
For inference content covered by OpenRouter’s ZDR policy, we do not retain prompts or responses after processing, except when you explicitly choose to have us store them or when retention is needed for CSAM review, reporting, and related legal preservation.
These CSAM provisions do not authorize general retention of ZDR inference content for unrelated purposes. OpenRouter’s commitment not to use inputs or outputs for model training continues (OpenRouter’s Privacy Policy).
Reporting and preservation requirements
CSAM reporting and preservation duties are established legal obligations. ZDR does not remove those duties.
Under U.S. law, covered providers must report to NCMEC’s CyberTipline as soon as reasonably possible after obtaining actual knowledge of facts or circumstances indicating specified apparent offenses. Reported contents and certain related contextual material must be preserved for one year after submission. That requirement applies to reported material, rather than every item flagged for review (18 U.S.C. § 2258A(a) and (h)).
Provider policies may differ
Model labs and providers may use different screening and retention methods. Some may retain content for a period of time to run automated safety checks before anything has been flagged. Those practices are separate from OpenRouter’s in-flight screening and are governed by the applicable model and provider policies.
OpenRouter documents provider policies so users can understand the requirements that apply to their requests. Review those policies when choosing a model or provider, especially if your organization has specific data-retention requirements.
Looking ahead
AI is opening up exciting possibilities, and the practices surrounding frontier models are evolving quickly. We’re updating our documentation and related terms to describe OpenRouter’s in-flight screening, possible retention of flagged content, and how provider policies are represented. As always, we will keep you informed.

report.summary: OpenRouter will screen all inference traffic in flight for child sexual abuse material, extending the check even to Zero Data Retention requests and retaining flagged content for human review.
report.background: OpenRouter is a routing layer that gives developers one API across hundreds of models from many labs, and its Zero Data Retention (ZDR) promise has been a selling point for privacy-sensitive teams. But aggregation makes it a chokepoint: regulators and law enforcement increasingly expect any service handling user-generated images or text — including generative AI — to run basic child-safety measures. NCMEC recommends hash matching plus classifiers, and U.S. law (18 U.S.C. § 2258A) obliges covered providers to report apparent CSAM to the CyberTipline and preserve related material for a year. Meanwhile, model labs and upstream providers already run their own screening with differing retention rules, so OpenRouter is standardising its layer and documenting the gaps.
key_points: Every inference request passing through OpenRouter is now screened in flight, not batched afterwards. Screening combines hash matching against digital fingerprints of previously identified CSAM with classifiers that flag suspected new material not yet in any hash database — the two-measure approach NCMEC recommends for services handling images and video.

Zero Data Retention is being redefined. OpenRouter's ZDR policy will still mean no training on your data and no retention after processing, with one explicit carve-out: content flagged as potential CSAM may be kept for review, reporting and legal preservation. The company stresses this does not authorise general retention for other purposes.

A flag is not a verdict. OpenRouter says a match indicates suspected material only, but flagged content — including non-hash matches — may be retained and passed to human reviewers, then reported to NCMEC's CyberTipline where the law requires, with reported material preserved for one year.

Legal duties override product promises. The post is explicit that CSAM reporting and preservation are statutory obligations and that ZDR does not remove them, which is why terms and documentation are being rewritten rather than just the pipeline.

Upstream providers differ. Some model labs retain content for a period to run automated safety checks before anything is flagged; those practices sit outside OpenRouter's in-flight screening and are governed by each provider's own policy, which OpenRouter now documents for users.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this marks the moment gateway and aggregator layers become compliance enforcement points, not just billing and routing convenience. Any intermediary reselling access to many models now inherits screening duties, and 'zero retention' will need precise, lawyer-readable definitions. Expect similar announcements from other routers and inference platforms, and pressure on smaller providers to adopt hash sharing. For developers, the practical impact is procurement: teams with strict data-residency or confidentiality requirements must re-read DPAs, assume flagged prompts may be human-reviewed, and consider self-hosted models or direct provider contracts for sensitive workloads. False positives are a real operational risk for medical, legal and security-research use cases. For regular users, safety improves marginally, but the implicit promise that a privacy-branded API means nobody ever looks at your prompts no longer holds.
report.tools: To follow up: read OpenRouter's privacy policy, ZDR documentation and per-provider policy pages before choosing a model. NCMEC's CyberTipline materials and hash-sharing programmes (authorisation required) explain the legal backdrop; Microsoft PhotoDNA and Thorn's Safer are the commercial detection standards. For teams wanting control, self-managed gateways such as LiteLLM, Portkey or Kong AI Gateway let you own logging and screening, and local inference via Ollama or vLLM keeps traffic off third-party routers entirely. Open-source image and text classifiers on Hugging Face can support your own pre-screening.
